questiontext.text: Storing a binary tree in a 1-based array, the children of the node at index i are at which indices?

feedback.text: Correct — left child at 2i, right child at 2i+1.
No — that is not how a heap-style array indexes children.
No — i/2 gives the parent, not the children.
No — with 1-based indexing the children are 2i and 2i+1.

generalfeedback.text: With 1-based indexing, node i has children at 2i (left) and 2i+1 (right); no pointers are needed.

questiontext.text: In a 1-based array representation, the parent of the node at index i is at which index?

feedback.text: Correct — integer division of i by 2 gives the parent.
No — 2i is the left child, not the parent.
No — that is the previous array slot, not the parent.
No — 2i+1 is the right child.

generalfeedback.text: Parent(i) = ⌊i/2⌋, the inverse of the child formulas 2i and 2i+1.

answer.text: A complete (or nearly complete) binary tree, such as a heap

feedback.text: Correct — complete trees leave no gaps in the array.

answer.text: A long skewed tree that is essentially a linked list

feedback.text: No — a skewed tree wastes enormous amounts of array space.

answer.text: A sparse tree with many missing nodes

feedback.text: No — missing nodes still consume reserved array slots.

answer.text: A general tree of arbitrary degree

feedback.text: No — the 2i/2i+1 scheme is for binary trees.

generalfeedback.text: Because a complete tree packs tightly with no holes, the array wastes no slots — which is exactly why heaps use it.

questiontext.text: What is the main drawback of the array representation?

answer.text: It wastes space for sparse or skewed trees

feedback.text: Correct — missing nodes still reserve array slots, so gaps are wasteful.

generalfeedback.text: A skewed or sparse tree of height h can require up to 2^(h+1)-1 slots for only a few nodes, wasting memory.
